*Figures below are drawn from the full report (`report_nedlame_treatment_comparison.html`), which has the complete methodology, caveats, and charts. This is a summary for discussion, not a standalone analysis.*

## The pilot, in brief

The farm is piloting a Nedap camera-based mobility alert. When the system flags a cow, DairyComp records a **`NEDLAME`** event; the cow is then assigned to one of two arms — **TX**, trimmed automatically off the alert, or **Control**, where staff decide whether and when to act.

718 cows have received a `NEDLAME` alert over a ~9-week window (2026-06-02 to 2026-08-03), the system's full history to date. Of those, **126 are excluded from the TX-vs-Control comparisons below** — their alert almost certainly reflects a post-trim gait change rather than an independent catch (explained in the next section) — leaving an analysis cohort of **592**: **262 TX** and **330 Control**. Every finding below is an early read on a still-young pilot, presented descriptively; there is no significance testing here, deliberately.

Alerts come in three types, used throughout: **`LOW`** (an absolute mobility score in the lowest band), **`LOW DECLINE`**, and **`STRONG DECLINE`** (a drop relative to that cow's own recent history). These are three different triggers with different enrollment rules, not simply three severity levels.

## A timing artifact in how alerts reach DairyComp, and two eligibility errors it exposed

A close read of one case turned up a real pattern: **`NEDLAME`'s daily batch import stamps each alert with the day it was *loaded* (~5am), not necessarily the day the underlying sensor event happened** — and trim records are commonly entered a day or two late (correctly backdated). The result: some alerts that fire 1-7 days *after* a trim aren't the camera making an independent catch — they're the camera picking up that cow's own post-treatment soreness/altered gait. Herd-wide, **204 of 957 `NEDLAME` alert-days (21.3%) fall within 14 days after a trim**. Cows whose *first* alert fits this pattern are now excluded from the analysis cohort and reported separately in the report's "Excluded" section.

The strongest evidence that these are artifacts rather than real new problems: **81% of the excluded cows never had another lameness event of any kind for the rest of that lactation** — nothing came of the alert.

Two further eligibility problems were found by cross-checking specific cows against their DairyComp cowcards, which is how essentially every real error in this analysis has surfaced:

- **A trim visit is often coded `LAME`, not `FOOTRIM`.** When the trimmer finds a lesion, that visit gets a `LAME` code and no separate `FOOTRIM` code — so any check looking only for `FOOTRIM`/`TRIM` misses exactly the trims that matter most. Correcting this grew the post-trim exclusion to **126 cows**, leaving a cohort of **592 (262 TX / 330 Control)** out of 718 ever alerted.
- **31 lesion cases were heifers who had never freshened** (lactation 0). A cow who has never calved was never eligible for NEDLAME's production-linked monitoring in the first place — the same reasoning as the report's existing dry-off exclusion, applied at the other end of a lactation. All 31 had been counted as 100% misses; they are now excluded, leaving **387** qualifying lesion cases.

## Headline findings

1. **Milk production**: no clear separation between arms — TX 93.8% of baseline by day 30 vs. Control 93.6%, essentially tied.

2. **Time to next trim/lameness event**: TX reaches a subsequent trim/LAME event in 87.2% of cases within 30 days vs. 32.0% for Control — expected, since TX auto-trims. **About half of TX's first follow-up visits still find nothing** (54.6% trim-only/no lesion, vs. 43.1% for Control).

3. **Independent staff detection**: staff catch lame cows on their own at a similar rate regardless of arm (Control 18.8%, TX 20.6%) — the alert + auto-trim protocol isn't replacing staff vigilance, it's running alongside it. Staff catch `Strong Decline` alerts meaningfully more often than `Low Decline` ones in both arms (TX: 40% vs. 15.4%; Control: 29.1% vs. 14.4%).

4. **What NEDAP is missing** *(drawn from the whole herd, not the cohort above)*: across the whole herd, **64.6% of lesion diagnoses since June 1 weren't caught by a NEDLAME alert first** — read this as an upper bound on true technology failure, not a precise figure, for the reasons below. (Cases too recently trimmed/diagnosed, already dried off, or on a not-yet-fresh heifer are excluded entirely, since NEDAP couldn't structurally alert in any of those situations.) The single largest component is cows that **genuinely never received an alert at all: 188 of 387 qualifying cases (49%)**. A further 42 cases had an alert that was excluded as a post-trim artifact, and the rest were alerted but not in time.

   **The TX-vs-Control split within this section should not be read as a treatment effect.** It looks dramatic (7.4% missed for TX, n=94, vs. 20.6% for Control, n=63), but it is largely mechanical: TX cows are auto-trimmed after their alert, so the trim the alert triggered is frequently the very visit at which their lesion is diagnosed — which scores the alert as "catching" it. TX cows accordingly generate a qualifying lesion case at nearly twice Control's rate (36% vs 19% of each arm), and about half of TX's "catches" are diagnosed within 3 days of the alert. The comparison also rests on just 7 TX misses and 13 Control misses. **The overall miss rate is the number worth quoting from this section; the arm split is not.**

   **Staff aren't fully backstopping the misses either**: of the 250 DairyComp-recorded misses, only 45 (18.0%) had a farm staff check (`CHKLAME`) in the week before diagnosis. (That 250 is the full recorded set — it deliberately includes the pipeline losses and enrollment gaps described next, because the question here is what the herd record shows, not what the sensor did.)

   A raw Nedap sensor export separates a *true* sensor miss from a case where the sensor fired but the flag never reached DairyComp. For the window that export covers (2025-08-25 to 2026-07-16), of the **194** DC-recorded misses inside it, **71 (36.6%) actually had the sensor fire in time** — a pipeline/integration gap, not a detection failure — leaving **123** true misses at the sensor level. **Roughly a third of what looks like a NEDAP miss in DairyComp is really a data-pipeline problem, not a sensor problem**, at least in the checkable window. (93 more recent lesion cases fall after the export's coverage ends and can't be checked yet.)

   **Two further checks narrow that "pipeline loss" figure, in opposite directions.** First: **18 of the 250 misses (7.2%) involve a cow absent from Nedap's SmartSight platform** (the separate instance used for mobility monitoring, distinct from the Activity platform staff use daily — all 18 are present on Activity). If that absence is real, those cows were never eligible to be caught at all. All 18 are first-lactation cows, which hints at an onboarding gap for newly-freshened heifers — **but this is unconfirmed**: the same pattern would appear if SmartSight's export simply omits very recently enrolled animals. Worth checking with Nedap before relying on it. Second, cutting the other way: DairyComp's enrollment rule for `Low`-type alerts is stricter than the sensor's own low-score threshold and specifically excludes cows with a history of upper-leg lameness — checking that against the 71 pipeline-loss cases found **at least 13 are likely correct by-design exclusions rather than pipeline bugs** (a floor, since the other half of that rule — the score at the time of the flag — isn't available in this data).

5. **Lameness history**: 39.9% of the cohort (236 of 592) carry a `Chronic` history label — still mostly an artifact of how chronicity is defined (any 2nd+ diagnosis more than a day apart) rather than evidence of active, recurring problems. Still only 3 cows total with a `Repeat` history label.

6. **Culling**: 16 of 330 Control cows (4.8%) and 12 of 262 TX cows (4.6%) have been culled so far — too close, and too early, to read as a treatment effect.

## What this suggests for discussion

- **The biggest single finding is how much of the "miss" gap is not a detection problem.** Four separate non-detection issues are now quantified: a sensor→DairyComp integration gap (~37% of checkable misses), the batch-load-timing artifact (126 of 718 alerted cows, 17.5%), a possible platform-enrollment gap (7.2% of misses, unconfirmed), and a by-design enrollment rule that shouldn't count as a failure at all (≥13 of 71 pipeline-loss cases). These are process and integration issues, and they're the natural first thing to raise with the Nedap/DairyComp integration team. **Separately, though, the largest single category of missed cases is still genuine sensor non-firing — 123 of the 194 checkable misses — which is a sensitivity question, not an integration one.** Both need attention; neither substitutes for the other.
- **Don't read TX's low Q4 miss rate as evidence the alerts perform better in that arm** (see finding 4) — the auto-trim protocol mechanically produces most of that difference, and the comparison rests on 7 vs 13 misses.
- The auto-trim protocol gets cows seen faster, at the cost of trimming a lot of cows who turn out fine — worth weighing against the labor/hoof-health cost of that over-trimming rate.
- Staff are already catching a meaningful share of lame cows on their own, alert or no alert — the pilot's main value-add may be less about replacing staff judgment and more about the cows staff *aren't* catching.
- The single biggest gap in DairyComp's own record is cows that never get a usable alert in the first place (188 of 387 cases, 49%). How much of that is true sensor failure versus pipeline or enrollment loss can only be answered for the window the raw sensor export covers, which ends 2026-07-16 — **a fresher export is the single most useful next data pull**, since it would let the same check run across the whole analysis period instead of roughly half of it.
- Everything here is based on ~9 weeks of `NEDLAME` history. Time-to-event and culling findings in particular will keep moving; the 62-day follow-up makes the culling comparison close to uninformative at this stage. Worth revisiting once there are a few more months on the clock.
